item.title: Deep Learning for Remote Sensing Image Superresolution: A comprehensive review and a new real-world benchmark
item.description: Single-image superresolution (SISR) is a long-standing research topic in the low-level vision of remote sensing. Its goal is to reconstruct a corresponding high-resolution (HR) image from a low-resolution (LR) image. In recent years, SISR for remote sensing has attracted widespread attention due to its potential applications in small object detection, land cover classification, and precision agriculture, and it has coincided with the rapid development of deep learning (DL) methods. However, a comprehensive review of these methods and real-world datasets remains lacking. To address this gap, this article systematically and comprehensively reviews DL-based SISR papers from the past decade. Specifically, we first introduce the various DL network architectures used. Second, we provide a comprehensive summary of SISR algorithms for optical remote sensing images (RSIs), including methodology, systematic comparisons, the evolution timeline, commonly used loss functions, remote sensing datasets, and evaluation metrics. To further promote the field of remote sensing SR, we propose a global-scale, versatile, and abundant dataset for real-world SR, L8S2PS-SR, which consists of 195 precisely aligned Landsat 8–Sentinel-2–PlanetScope satellite image pairs captured at different seasons and geographical locations. Furthermore, we implement 15 representative methods on publicly available datasets and our proposed L8S2PS-SR dataset to evaluate their performance. Finally, some challenges and future research directions in the field of remote sensing SISR are discussed, aiming to provide research ideas for researchers. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Meng-333/L8S2PS-SR.
item.authors: Fanen Meng;Sensen Wu;Yi Xiao;Qiangqiang Yuan;Zhiguo Jiang;Fengying Xie;Zhenhong Du;Haopeng Zhang;

item.title: MapYourCity: A New Multimodal Benchmark Dataset and Community Challenge: Building age estimation from street-view and satellite imagery
item.description: Estimating the construction year of buildings is critical for advancing sustainability, as older structures often lack energy-efficient features. Sustainable urban planning relies on accurate building age data to reduce energy consumption and mitigate climate change. In this work, we introduce MapYourCity, a novel multimodal benchmark dataset comprising top-view very high-resolution (VHR) imagery, multispectral Earth observation (EO) data from the Copernicus Sentinel-2 constellation, and co-localized street-view images across various European cities. Each building is labeled with its construction epoch, and the task is formulated as a seven-class classification problem covering periods from 1900 to the present. To advance research in EO generalization and multimodal learning, we organized a community-driven data challenge in 2024, hosted by the European Space Agency (ESA) $\Phi$-lab, which ran for four months and attracted wide participation. This article presents the top four performing models from the challenge and their evaluation results. We assess model generalization on cities excluded from training to prevent data leakage, and evaluate performance under missing modality scenarios, particularly when street-view data are unavailable. Results demonstrate that building age estimation is both feasible and effective, even in previously unseen cities and when relying solely on top-view satellite imagery (i.e. with VHR and Sentinel-2 images). The MapYourCity dataset thus provides a valuable resource for developing scalable, real-world solutions in sustainable urban analytics.
item.authors: Nikolaos Dionelis;Alessandra Feliciotti;Mattia Marconcini;Devis Peressutti;Nika Oman Kadunc;JaeWan Park;Hagai Raja Sinulingga;Steve Andreas Immanuel;Ba Tran;Caroline Arnold;Nicolas Longépé;

item.title: Lithosphere–Atmosphere–Ionosphere Coupling: Opportunities and challenges from phenomenon observation to physical prediction
item.description: Natural hazards (NHs), such as earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, generate disturbances that propagate through the atmosphere and ionosphere, leaving distinct signatures. The study of these ionospheric signatures has evolved into a promising interdisciplinary field. Over the past two decades, advancements in remote sensing technologies, particularly the GNSS, have significantly expanded our understanding of lithosphere–atmosphere–ionosphere coupling (LAIC) mechanisms. Recent studies indicate that, for some large coseismic and coeruptive events, ionospheric signatures may provide complementary constraints on source location and physical properties, suggesting their potential value for future near-real-time (NRT) monitoring and hazard assessment. Despite remarkable progress in this field, a significant scientific gap remains between the observation of postevent disturbances and the achievement of reliable prehazard forecasting. The core challenges lie in identifying weak signals of lithospheric activity amid strong background noise and establishing a unified theoretical framework. This article systematically reviews the development, key methodologies, and cutting-edge progress of LAIC research and proposes an integrated analytical framework of “technological evolution–signal separation–physical mechanisms.” This review demonstrates that coseismic ionospheric disturbances (CIDs), volcanic Lamb wave effects, and other coeruptive ionospheric disturbances now have a clearer physical interpretation and are amenable to quantitative analysis. However, for the much-debated preseismic ionospheric precursors, the reliability of signal identification and the unification of physical mechanisms remain weak links in current research. Ultimately, it is concluded that, for LAIC research to move from phenomenological correlation to physical prediction, it must address three core challenges: signal attribution, observational systems, and physical theory. Future breakthroughs will depend heavily on the synergistic development of physics-informed artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms, a trans-spheric coordinated observation system, and a unified, interpretable physical model.
item.authors: Wang Li;Fangsong Yang;Li Li;Dongsheng Zhao;Kefei Zhang;Xiaoqing Zuo;Andong Hu;Craig M. Hancock;Xiujiang Pan;

item.title: Uncrewed Aerial Vehicle-Based Ground-Penetrating Radar for 3D Subsurface Imaging: Electromagnetic modeling, tomographic processing, and open challenges
item.description: Ground-penetrating radar (GPR) systems mounted on uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) offer new opportunities for flexible and rapid subsurface mapping. However, several methodological and practical challenges arise, including the management of large amounts of data measured at points that are not evenly spaced along irregular flight trajectories and at nonnegligible distances from the air/soil interface. These factors affect the reliability of the surveys and, in practice, necessitate a careful optimization of the measurement configuration. Furthermore, ad hoc data processing strategies capable of producing reliable focused 3D images of the investigated scenario are required when the measurement height cannot be neglected with respect to the probing wavelength. This article presents a focused review and a critical analysis of electromagnetic modeling and data processing approaches for 3D UAV-based GPR imaging, with an emphasis on microwave tomographic formulations. Crucial issues, such as the definition of acquisition requirements, the impact of data sparsity on imaging performance, and computational efficiency, are discussed. Specific methodological approaches, supported by numerical simulations and experimental results, are analyzed in detail to highlight the achievable capabilities and limitations of UAV-based GPR imaging. Furthermore, open challenges and perspectives are addressed.
item.authors: Ilaria Catapano;Giuseppe Esposito;Gianluca Gennarelli;Francesco Soldovieri;

item.title: AI in Mangrove Remote Sensing: A comprehensive review
item.description: Mangroves, occupying the intertidal zones of tropical and subtropical coastlines, are vital ecosystems that stabilize shorelines and mitigate the impacts of natural disasters. Remote sensing has a long-standing history in mangrove research, and the recent rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has profoundly transformed this field. While several reviews have explored the applications of remote sensing in mangrove research, none have systematically focused on the role of AI and traced its evolution from current contributions to future trends. In this review, we provide a comprehensive synthesis of the application of AI in remote sensing-based mangrove research. We organize our review around three key research topics: spatial patterns, functional attributes, and environmental interactions. For each, we first provide a summary of non-AI approaches, and then we give a detailed overview of AI-driven studies, and finally analyze the changes brought by AI. We conclude that AI has transformed mangrove research by enhancing data utilization and integration, advancing the capacity to capture complex relationships, and expanding the scope and depth of research. We discuss challenges related to reference sample collection, model transferability, and process understanding, then make recommendations for future research focused on mapping spatial patterns with multimodal AI models, estimating functional attributes with physics-guided AI models, and modeling environmental interactions with explainable AI (XAI) models. We hope this review will provide a valuable reference for researchers and promote further advances in this field.
item.authors: Zhaohui Xue;Siyu Qian;Gustau Camps-Valls;Mingming Jia;Hongsheng Zhang;Kourosh Khoshelham;

item.title: Full-Waveform Lidar Remote Sensing for Shallow-Water Detection: Systems, signal processing algorithms, and applications
item.description: Accurate shallow-water bathymetry is critical for coastal management, navigation, and environmental monitoring. Traditional methods, such as shipborne single/multibeam sonar and passive optical (satellite or aerial imagery) techniques, suffer from limitations in very shallow zones and turbid waters. Airborne lidar bathymetry (ALB) uses a green (532-nm) laser to penetrate water and directly measure the seabed depth, overcoming many of these constraints. Modern ALB platforms—from NASA’s early Airborne Oceanographic Lidar (AOL) to NOAA’s Scanning Hydrographic Operational Airborne Lidar Survey (SHOALS) and Coastal Zone Mapping and Imaging Lidar (CZMIL) as well as commercial systems, like RIEGL’s VQ series and Leica/Airborne Hydrography AB (AHAB)’s Chiroptera—integrate high-energy pulsed lasers, inertial/GNSS navigation, and full-waveform digitizers to capture detailed subsurface profiles. Full-waveform recording retains the entire echo pulse shape, enabling advanced processing: it improves weak bottom echo detection, profiles water-column attenuation, and separates overlapping signals. Key challenges remain in full-waveform ALB (FW-ALB): bottom returns can be faint or overlapped by surface scattering, water-wave refraction errors must be corrected, and turbidity drastically reduces the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Emerging research trends address these issues via sophisticated waveform decomposition, stacking methods, multiwavelength scanning, and machine learning (ML) for signal classification. This review surveys the latest FW-ALB technology and algorithms and typical applications and identifies future directions, aiming to synthesize advances in sensor design, processing techniques, and practical bathymetric outcomes to guide ongoing development in shallow-water lidar bathymetry.
item.authors: Dongfang Zhang;Yifu Chen;Lizhe Wang;Lin Wu;Xiaohan Zhang;Yuan Le;

item.title: Remote Sensing Monitoring of Marine Plastic Litter: From macroplastics to microplastics
item.description: Marine plastic litter presents a pervasive and escalating threat to global marine ecosystems, which urgently requires effective monitoring techniques. Remote sensing offers significant potential for large-scale and repetitive monitoring. While remote sensing of macroplastics has demonstrated feasibility through direct detection, the monitoring of microplastics is constrained by the spatial resolution and radiometric sensitivity of remote sensors. Since direct detection of microplastics remains highly challenging, current approaches primarily rely on indirect environmental proxies. However, these proxy-based methods face key challenges arising from signal–background confusion, uncertain proxy origins, inconsistent proxy–plastic correspondence, and spatiotemporal scale inconsistencies. Consequently, we propose that future research should pivot toward proxy–background discrimination, proxy source discrimination, physics-informed proxy modeling, and spatiotemporal matching. The ultimate goal is to build a more robust and reliable monitoring framework, effectively bridging the gap “from macroplastics to microplastics.”
item.authors: Dayan Guan;Boyuan Zheng;Yanfeng Gu;Yu Tian;Wei Zhan;Lei Wang;Jun Zhou;

item.title: A Survey of Intelligent Change Detection Techniques for Hyperspectral Images Under Varying Supervision: Reliable reference points for method evaluation
item.description: Change detection (CD) holds significant value in fields such as environmental monitoring, disaster assessment, and resource surveys. Hyperspectral images (HSIs), with their rich spectral information, offer unique advantages for CD. The rise of deep learning has substantially propelled the flourishing development of HSICD. Model architectures have undergone continuous evolution, while learning paradigms have gradually expanded from supervised learning, which relies heavily on labeled data to encompass semisupervised and unsupervised approaches. Nevertheless, significant imaging differences, high redundancy and coarse spatial resolution, and the scarcity of annotations continue to pose challenges to the generalizability and robustness of the existing models. To systematically analyze intelligent CD technologies and challenges, this article comprehensively reviews deep learning-based intelligent HSICD methods, focusing on the comparative analysis of learning strategies under different supervision information. Furthermore, it consolidates widely used datasets and performance benchmarks within the field to provide reliable reference points for method evaluation while also exploring key future development directions. This review aims to offer theoretical underpinnings and directional guidance for further research in HSICD, thereby advancing the role of remote sensing (RS) change interpretation techniques.
item.authors: Tianyuan Zhou;Fulin Luo;Meiqi Hu;Chuan Fu;Tan Guo;Bo Du;Jocelyn Chanussot;Liangpei Zhang;

item.title: Evaluating Machine Learning Emulators for Atmospheric Radiative Transfer: The Atmospheric Machine Learning Emulation Challenge
item.description: The Atmospheric Machine Learning Emulation Challenge (AMLEC) provided a benchmark for evaluating machine learning approaches to emulating atmospheric radiative transfer models (RTMs). Participants were tasked with predicting spectral data across two scenarios involving different input variables and spectral configurations: 1) atmospheric correction of hyperspectral satellite data and 2) carbon dioxide (CO2) concentration retrieval. Several training datasets, spanning realistic input ranges and containing 500–10,000 samples each, were used. Testing included interpolation and extrapolation to out-of-range conditions. Eight models were submitted, spanning neural networks (NNs) (four) and Gaussian processes (GPs) (four) with various configurations. The results showed that GP approaches achieved the lowest errors under scarce data conditions, while complex NNs proved competitive when sufficient training data were available. Beyond scientific insights, AMLEC-1 fostered community engagement, reproducible workflows, and open data sharing. This article summarizes the competition design, datasets, evaluation metrics, and key findings, providing lessons for future benchmarks at the intersection of atmospheric science and machine learning.
item.authors: Jorge Vicent Servera;Jasdeep Singh;Axel Rochel;Julio Cesar Contreras Huerta;Romain Poirier;Panagiotis Liatsis;Hasan Al Marzouqi;Gustau Camps-Valls;

item.title: Remote Sensing Image Intelligent Interpretation From a Language-Centered Perspective: Principles, methods, and challenges
item.description: Remote sensing image interpretation has predominantly followed a visual-centered paradigm, relying on visual feature extraction to achieve semantic understanding. However, faced with increasingly complex interpretation demands, such methods have inherent limitations in cross-modal reasoning, abstract semantic representation, and decision-making. Although large language models (LLMs) have recently been applied to the remote sensing domain, existing research focuses mostly on performance improvements in specific downstream tasks and lacks a systematic theoretical explanation of the core role of language in the cognitive process. This review aims to reveal the paradigm shift in remote sensing interpretation from “visual-centered” to “language-centered.” Inspired by global workspace theory (GWT) in cognitive science, we construct a language-centered remote sensing interpretation framework. This framework positions the LLM as a cognitive hub, coordinating the four spaces of perception, task, knowledge, and action, thereby aiming to achieve a unified loop of understanding, reasoning, and decision-making. We first analyze the potential of LLMs as core cognitive components and then systematically review key challenges in realizing this paradigm: multimodal representation, knowledge association and reasoning, and decision-making and execution. To address these challenges, we summarize existing solutions, training datasets and evaluation benchmarks. Finally, we outline future research directions regarding the adaptive alignment of multimodal data, task understanding under dynamic knowledge constraints, trustworthy reasoning, and autonomous interaction. This review aims to provide a theoretical perspective for understanding the role of language in remote sensing cognition and to serve as a reference for building next-generation intelligent cognitive geospatial analysis systems.
item.authors: Haifeng Li;Wang Guo;Haiyang Wu;Mengwei Wu;Jipeng Zhang;Qing Zhu;Yu Liu;Xin Huang;Chao Tao;

item.title: A Review of Onboard AI Technologies for Synthetic Aperture Radar: Techniques, challenges, and opportunities
item.description: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) has become one of the most vital satellite imaging modalities for Earth observation (EO) due to its 24-h all-weather imaging capability. Processing SAR data on board can aid multiple time-sensitive critical use cases. With advancements in signal processing techniques and deep learning (DL), detecting insights directly from SAR images on board rather than downlinking them for ground processing is a viable headway. However, SAR data are massive compared to their optical counterparts and processing such colossal numbers of data in onboard computers poses considerable challenges. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of onboard SAR data processing using artificial intelligence (AI), covering the steps in the processing pipeline, from the payloads that source SAR data, to the acquisition, triage, and preprocessing of product formation for deriving actionable insights. It also explores how the applications of SAR processing in security, surveillance, environmental monitoring, and disaster management can utilize onboard AI, emphasizing the need for low-latency, task-specific solutions with modest memory and compute footprints that fit in onboard size, weight, and power (SWaP). The contributions of key industry players and space agencies, such as ICEYE, Capella Space, the European Space Agency’s (ESA’s) $\Phi$-lab, the German Aerospace Center (DLR), and NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), in advancing onboard SAR capabilities are also highlighted. The article addresses critical challenges, including hardware limitations, power efficiency, and real-time data handling, and promising solutions such as various model optimization techniques, hardware acceleration, and continual AI training. A forward-looking perspective is presented, focusing on bounded-latency inferencing and progressive automation to achieve an efficient onboard AI pipeline for SAR data. This work highlights the transformative potential of AI in enabling efficient, accurate, and scalable onboard SAR data processing for critical applications.
item.authors: Pretha Sur;Anonnya Ghosh;Ibrahim Hossain;Moloud Abdar;Abbas Khosravi;Nermine Hendy;Roberto Del Prete;Ryszard Kowalczyk;Andrew Barton;Biplab Banerjee;

item.title: Data-Driven Vision-Language Models for Remote Sensing: A survey
item.description: During the deep learning era, innovations in remote sensing (RS) vision models primarily focused on optimizing network architectures for specific tasks and conducting end-to-end training. However, with the advent of the vision-language models (VLMs) era, constrained by substantial computational resource demands, the mainstream research paradigm has shifted toward adapting general-purpose VLMs using RS vertical domain data for fine-tuning, rather than modifying their core architectures. This transition marks a change in the innovation pathway from model centric to data centric. Despite the increasing importance of data, the academic community still lacks a systematic data-centric survey to guide researchers in constructing high-quality RS vision-language datasets for various application scenarios and in conducting effective model fine-tuning and performance evaluation based on these datasets. To address this gap, this article presents a systematic review of the development status of RS datasets tailored for VLMs. It further provides a comprehensive practical guide for RS researchers in the large model era, covering the entire pipeline from data construction to fine-tuning and evaluation. This article aims to encourage the academic community to build more diverse and higher-quality vision-language datasets for specialized RS subfields. Ultimately, the goal is to converge these efforts into a comprehensive RS vision-language corpus that offers extensive task coverage and a wide geographical distribution, thereby laying a solid data foundation for advancing toward general artificial intelligence (AI) in RS.
item.authors: Yue Zhou;Shujun Zhao;Xue Yang;Ruigang Li;Tianwen Zhang;Mengcheng Lan;Chaofeng Chen;Lingfei Ma;Hongjie He;Jonathan Li;

item.title: HyperCap: A hyperspectral land-cover captioning dataset for vision–language models
item.description: We introduce HyperCap, the first large-scale hyperspectral captioning dataset designed to enhance model performance and effectiveness in remote sensing applications. Unlike traditional hyperspectral imaging (HSI) benchmarks, HyperCap integrates spectral data with pixelwise textual annotations, enabling deeper semantic understanding. This dataset enhances model performance in tasks like classification and feature extraction, providing a valuable resource for advanced remote sensing applications. HyperCap is constructed from four benchmark datasets and annotated through a hybrid approach combining automated and manual methods to ensure accuracy and consistency. Empirical evaluations using state-of-the-art encoders and diverse fusion techniques demonstrate significant improvements in classification performance. These results underscore the potential of vision–language learning in HSI and position HyperCap as a foundational dataset for future research in the field. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/arya-domain/HyperCap.
item.authors: Aryan Das;Tanishq Rachamalla;Pravendra Singh;Koushik Biswas;Vinay Kumar Verma;Salvador Garcia;Antonio Plaza;Swalpa Kumar Roy;

item.title: Atmospheric Methane Monitoring Using Satellites: Bibliometric and visual analytics
item.description: As the world’s second-largest greenhouse gas, methane has a global warming potential more than 28 times greater than that of carbon dioxide. Consequently, reducing methane emissions is considered one of the most effective short-term mitigation strategies for addressing global warming. To achieve this goal, the accurate identification of methane emission sources is critically important. Methane monitoring serves as a fundamental basis for pinpointing emission sources and supporting the implementation of mitigation actions. Currently, methane monitoring primarily relies on three principal approaches: ground-based observations, aerial monitoring, and satellite remote sensing. Among these, satellite remote sensing technology, owing to its advantages of wide coverage, high spatiotemporal continuity, and noncontact observation, has gradually overcome the limitations of traditional ground-based monitoring in spatial representativeness, coverage breadth, and cost efficiency. It has become an essential tool for monitoring methane emissions, quantifying methane emission sources and sinks, and evaluating the effectiveness of emission reduction measures at both global and regional scales. This study systematically reviews academic progress in the monitoring of atmospheric methane using satellite remote sensing techniques. Based on 621 relevant publications from the Web of Science database, bibliometric and visualization-based methods were employed to analyze research trends in satellite-based methane remote sensing. First, currently available satellite sensors used for methane monitoring were systematically cataloged. Second, influential core publications, key authors, leading countries, institutions, and journals within the field were identified and visually analyzed. Furthermore, by analyzing the citation structures of referenced articles, authors, and journals, the theoretical foundations and primarily knowledge sources of this research were revealed. Additionally, through keyword evolution paths and co-occurrence networks, the developmental trajectory of satellite-based methane remote sensing research and its projected future trends were traced. The findings of this analysis aim to provide researchers with comprehensive insights into the current state of the field and practical guidance for identifying future research directions.
item.authors: Botao He;Yong Xue;Wenhao Liu;Pei Li;Peng Wang;Liying Han;Kaiyuan Li;

item.title: Mitigating Topographic Effects in Optical Remote Sensing: From surface reflectance to high-level products
item.description: Accurate estimation of environmental variables from satellite observations in mountainous terrain remains challenging, as complex topography systematically alters the sun–target–sensor geometry. These terrain-induced distortions, including slope–aspect effects, shadowing, and terrain obstruction, are largely ignored by most operational satellite products. Given that mountainous regions occupy approximately 24% of the Earth’s land surface, these errors introduce globally substantial uncertainties. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of topographic correction and topography-aware strategies based on a retrieval chain. We reviewed the progress in reducing topographic impacts in surface reflectance in three strategies: (i) empirical and semi-empirical methods, (ii) physically-based radiative transfer correction methods, and (iii) combined atmospheric–topographic correction schemes. Furthermore, we critically examine the propagation of topographic effects and specific mitigation strategies across three key downstream domains: (i) surface radiation budget components (e.g., albedo, shortwave/longwave radiation, and land surface temperature (LST)); (ii) biophysical variables (e.g., vegetation indices, leaf area index (LAI), fraction of absorbed photosynthetically active radiation (FAPAR), and gross primary production (GPP)); and (iii) geophysical variables (specifically snow cover and evapotranspiration). A general assessment identifies two primary strategies for estimating high-level surface parameters: a sequential approach that estimates variables from pre-topographically corrected surface reflectance, and an integrated inversion approach that explicitly couples topographic effects within the retrieval framework. Current research is increasingly shifting toward the latter to ensure better physical consistency and accuracy. However, a significant gap persists between these sophisticated algorithms and operational global products (e.g., standard MODIS/Landsat pipelines), which largely retain flat-terrain assumptions. Despite methodological progress, persistent challenges include deep-shadow recovery, sensitivity to DEM resolution, and the scarcity of in-situ validation data. We conclude by outlining research priorities, advocating for physics-informed AI and foundation models, and expanding validation networks to facilitate reliable global monitoring of mountainous ecosystems.
item.authors: Yichuan Ma;Shunlin Liang;Tao He;Jianguang Wen;Ainong Li;Han Ma;Yunjun Yao;Jianglei Xu;Wenyuan Li;Yuxiang Zhang;

item.title: Deep Learning in Geophysical Electromagnetic Inversion: A review
item.description: Innovative inversion methods are pivotal for optimizing imaging and interpretation in geophysical exploration. Deep learning (DL) has emerged as a transformative solution, leveraging hierarchical abstractions to overcome the efficiency bottlenecks of traditional numerical methods. Recent studies demonstrate that DL accelerates computational workflows by orders of magnitude—achieving speedups of 200–350×, particularly in 3D forward modeling tasks—while maintaining high reconstruction accuracy (>95% consistency with true models) for specific structured inversion scenarios. This success has fostered a data-driven paradigm that complements classical physics-based optimization. This review article systematically summarizes the latest advancements in DL-based geophysical electromagnetic (EM) inversion. We delineate the algorithmic foundations and detail core application strategies addressing critical challenges, including computational efficiency, complex medium imaging, and the integration of physical laws. Finally, we critically assess current limitations and propose a prioritized research agenda for the future of intelligent inversion.
item.authors: Xingran Guo;Tiaojie Xiao;Xinhai Chen;Hongzhu Cai;Jie Liu;Keqin Li;

item.title: Remote Sensing for Understanding the Vertical Dimension of Urban Landscapes: A review on data, products, methods, and prospects
item.description: Quantifying the vertical structure of urban landscapes is the prerequisite to understanding its social and ecological impacts. Remote sensing provides an important tool for data acquisition and pattern analysis on the vertical structure of urban landscapes. Therefore, a comprehensive review of how remote sensing can facilitate the quantification of the vertical structure of urban landscapes is desirable not only for the remote sensing community but also for the increasing number of scholars who are broadly interested in 3D-related issues. Here, we present a comprehensive review of the current statuses of data, products, methods, and applications for quantifying the vertical dimension of urban landscapes using remote sensing. We further discuss the current challenges and future research needed. Specifically, we first review and compare the remote sensing data that could be used to extract the vertical information of urban landscapes, including passive optical data, lidar data, synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data, and street view imagery. We then presented a detailed list of the digital surface model (DSM) and ground object height products derived from remotely sensed data that are readily used for quantifying the vertical structure of urban landscapes, ranging from global-scale products to local ones with finer resolution. We also review key approaches for urban vertical structure analysis, including urban land cover classification, analysis of the vertical structure of urban architectures, green spaces, and comprehensive landscapes, and also analysis of the dynamics of urban vertical structures. Additionally, we have synthesized applications of urban vertical structures in six core fields: urban heat islands and microclimates, disaster risks, biodiversity, energy and resource consumption, human settlements and social equity, and urban management and planning. Finally, we discuss current challenges and future opportunities, such as limitations and tradeoffs of remote sensing technologies for vertical analysis, extracting vertical information by fusing multisource remote sensing data, deep learning for high-resolution and high-quality DSM generation, establishing a comprehensive index system for urban vertical structure quantification, monitoring the dynamics of 3D urban landscapes based on long-time-series data, exploring the human perception of 3D urban landscapes, and addressing uncertainty and robustness. To our knowledge, this article is the first work that comprehensively integrates these elements around the urban vertical structure. It provides abundant information on the quantification of the vertical structure of urban landscapes using remote sensing and offers valuable insights for the remote sensing and 3D research community.
item.authors: Haiming Qin;Weiqi Zhou;Zhe Zhu;Qihao Weng;

item.title: Artificial Intelligence for Wildfire Monitoring in North Africa: A decade of remote sensing research (2015–2025)
item.description: Wildfires pose an increasing threat to ecosystems, infrastructure, and human livelihoods across North Africa, where Mediterranean and arid environments intersect under intensifying climatic stress. Over the past decade, advances in machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL) and satellite remote sensing (RS) have substantially improved wildfire detection, burned-area mapping, and fire-risk modeling. However, most existing reviews of artificial intelligence–based wildfire monitoring focus on North America, Australia, and southern Europe, with limited attention to North African contexts. This article presents a systematic regional review of ML and DL approaches for wildfire monitoring in North Africa from 2015 to 2025. Following a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA)-inspired scoping methodology, we synthesize peer-reviewed studies that employ Earth observation (EO) data for active fire detection, burned-area and severity mapping, fire occurrence prediction, and postfire ecosystem analysis. We examine commonly used satellite datasets (e.g., MODIS, VIIRS, Sentinel-2, Landsat), model families [including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), spatiotemporal architectures, and emerging transformer-based models], and data-fusion strategies integrating multisensor and ancillary information. Beyond cataloguing methods, the review highlights region-specific challenges, such as limited ground-truth data availability, eco-regional domain shift, validation fragility, and infrastructure constraints. We identify emerging solutions, including transfer learning, weak and semisupervised labeling, and the adaptation of EO foundation models. Finally, we outline future research directions toward standardized regional benchmarks, explainable and scalable DL pipelines, and systematic evaluation of globally trained models and transfer-learning strategies for North African deployment.
item.authors: Nicola Aimane Dimarco;Ibtissam Faraji;Miriam Wahbi;Hakim Boulaassal;Mustapha Maatouk;Otman Yazidi Aalaoui;Omar EL Kharki;

item.title: Distributed Scatterer Interferometry From Traditional Methods to Deep Learning: A comprehensive review
item.description: Interferometric synthetic aperture radar (InSAR) enables high-precision measurement of Earth surface deformation, providing essential support for geohazard monitoring and geophysical parameter retrieval. However, long-term monitoring is challenged by temporal decorrelation, which can significantly degrade the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the interferometric phase. To overcome this challenge, distributed scatterer (DS) interferometry (DSI) reconstructs a temporally consistent phase series by leveraging redundant interferograms. Over the past 15 years, traditional model-based methods have undergone steady refinement, while the recent introduction of deep learning techniques into this field has injected new vitality. This article provides a comprehensive review of both traditional model-based and emerging deep learning-driven approaches. Specifically, we review the complete DSI processing workflow, including homogeneous pixel selection, complex coherence estimation, interferometric phase series estimation, and DS identification. For each stage, representative methods from both traditional and learning-based approaches are analyzed, supported by simulated and real-data experiments. Finally, we summarize the strengths and limitations of existing techniques, identify current challenges, and outline promising directions for future research. This article aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of DSI and to inspire further research in this vibrant and rapidly evolving field.
item.authors: Changjun Zhao;Hanwen Yu;Mi Jiang;
